You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they turn guesses into promises. A team identifies a problem, imagines a solution, estimates the work, and places a feature on a timeline. By the time that timeline reaches executives or customers, the uncertainty has disappeared. What began as “we think this might help” becomes “this will ship in September.”

That shift changes how teams behave. Instead of asking whether an idea is still worth pursuing, they ask how to deliver it on schedule. New evidence becomes an inconvenience. A customer interview that challenges the original assumption is treated as a threat to the plan rather than a reason to improve it. The roadmap starts protecting decisions that should still be open to question.

Many roadmaps also confuse activity with progress. Launching a dashboard, rebuilding onboarding, or adding an integration sounds concrete, but none of those things is inherently valuable. Their value depends on what changes for users and the business. When success means shipping the promised feature, teams can complete the roadmap without solving the problems that justified it.

Then there is the problem of competing interests. Sales wants features that close deals. Support wants fewer recurring complaints. Executives want visible moves into new markets. Engineering wants time to fix fragile systems. Each concern may be legitimate, but putting all of them on one timeline does not create a strategy. It often creates a compromise in which everything matters and nothing receives enough attention.

The calendar adds another distortion. Product work includes discovery, technical surprises, dependencies, and feedback that cannot be scheduled precisely months in advance. Yet roadmaps frequently present distant work with the same confidence as work already underway. Teams respond by padding estimates, cutting scope, or quietly sacrificing quality. The dates survive while the intended value shrinks.

A useful roadmap makes choices visible without pretending the future is settled. It explains which problems matter, why they matter now, and what evidence would justify continuing, changing direction, or stopping. It distinguishes genuine commitments from possibilities and becomes less specific as it looks further ahead.

This does not mean abandoning deadlines or accountability. Some dates are real, and teams need to coordinate. But accountability should include noticing when a plan is wrong, not just executing it faithfully.

Most roadmaps fail when people expect them to remove uncertainty rather than help manage it. A roadmap earns its place when it helps a team decide what to do next, including when to leave an old idea behind.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they treat the future as something we can schedule. Teams spend weeks lining up features and dates as if they already know what customers will need six months from now and how long every piece of work will take. Then the world moves. A new competitor appears, a key assumption turns out to be wrong, or someone important leaves the company. The carefully drawn plan starts looking like fiction.

People also turn the roadmap into a commitment instead of a working hypothesis. Sales uses the dates to close deals. Leadership uses the document to judge whether the team is delivering. When the inevitable changes happen, trust disappears. The thing that was supposed to keep everyone aligned becomes the thing everyone argues about.

A lot of roadmaps describe solutions rather than the problems worth solving. They become a list of screens and capabilities decided last quarter. Fresh evidence shows up, but the team keeps executing the old list because changing the roadmap feels like admitting failure. The document stops helping people think and starts telling them what to build no matter what they learn.

We consistently underestimate complexity. Work takes longer than the slides suggested. Dependencies surface late. Maintenance and technical debt that were never on the roadmap suddenly demand attention. Discovery that would reduce risk gets skipped because it does not look like progress against the published plan.

Communication gaps finish the job. The group that created the roadmap rarely stays in close conversation with the people building the product or talking to customers every day. Hidden assumptions stay hidden until they blow up. Trade-offs that should have been explicit stay implicit until it is too late.

The roadmaps that survive are the ones treated as living sketches rather than finished paintings. They stay detailed only for the near term and stay deliberately vague further out. They get revised often. They focus more on the outcomes the business needs than on the exact features that might produce those outcomes. Most companies do not operate that way. They produce a clean looking artifact, present it, and then wonder why it did not last. Planning gives the comforting feeling of control. That feeling is usually an illusion, and that is why most product roadmaps fail.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: Repeated negative parallelism (Tell 1: 'threat to the plan rather than a reason', 'does not create a strategy. It often creates a compromise', 'not just executing it faithfully', 'remove uncertainty rather than help manage it')
Frequent triads (Tell 6: 'dashboard, onboarding, or integration'; 'padding estimates, cutting scope, or quietly sacrificing quality'; 'continuing, changing direction, or stopping')
Formulaic nuance paragraph and uplifting resolution where every point lands cleanly (Tell 17: 'This does not mean abandoning deadlines...')
tells_B: Blatant recap ending echoing the prompt verbatim (Tell 4: '...and that is why most product roadmaps fail.')
Relentless short, punchy sentence rhythm (Tell 9: 'Then the world moves.', 'Dependencies surface late.', 'Communication gaps finish the job.', 'They get revised often.')
Multiple instances of negative parallelism (Tell 1: 'commitment instead of a working hypothesis', 'solutions rather than the problems worth solving', 'living sketches rather than finished paintings')
Triad of clauses (Tell 6: 'A new competitor appears, a key assumption turns out to be wrong, or someone important leaves the company')
